results.title: packet.ai vs CoreWeave: GPU Cloud Comparison 2026 | packet.ai
highlights:
CoreWeave is the hyperscaler of the neoclouds. packet.ai is the opposite end of the same market. They rarely compete for the same purchase order, which is exactly why the comparison is useful.

Author
: packet.ai Team
Updated
: September 2, 2026
Category
: Comparison

CoreWeave went public, signed multi-billion-dollar capacity deals and builds Kubernetes-native GPU infrastructure for the largest AI labs and enterprises. Its on-demand catalogue is priced per 8-GPU node, its committed-use discounts run to 60%, and its published H100 and B200 rates sit closer to AWS than to RunPod.

packet.ai is a single-card-up cloud. You can rent one RTX 4090 for $0.39/hr or one B200 for $3.75/hr, no contract. This comparison is for teams who have outgrown a laptop GPU, are getting CoreWeave's name in vendor shortlists, and want to know whether that scale is something they actually need yet.

### What CoreWeave offers

CoreWeave's published on-demand rates in August 2026, normalised per GPU from 8-GPU instances: HGX H100 $6.16/hr (spot $2.46), HGX H200 $6.31/hr (spot $2.62), HGX B200 $8.60/hr ($68.80 for the node, spot $4.26), A100 80GB SXM $2.70/hr, GB200 NVL72 $10.50/hr. RTX Pro 6000 is listed at $2.50/hr on reserved terms. Egress is free.

- Kubernetes-native (CKS), managed Slurm on Kubernetes (SUNK), Tensorizer, high-performance object and file storage
- Committed-use discounts up to 60%; most revenue is multi-year contracts
- Spot capacity at roughly 40% of on-demand for interruptible work
- 8-GPU nodes are the default unit; single-GPU on-demand is limited

...

CoreWeave is built for the multi-year, 8-GPU-node customer: reserved GB200 NVL72 racks, CKS Kubernetes, SUNK-managed Slurm, and committed-use discounts up to 60% for teams that sign long contracts. That is a real, well-built platform for a specific buyer. It is not built for a team that wants one GPU today without a sales call.

packet.ai is exactly that: single-card on-demand, published rates, no contract. On the card both platforms sell at comparable scale, packet.ai's A100 80GB Dedicated is $1.43/hr against CoreWeave's $2.70/hr on-demand SXM rate, a 47% gap. The B200 comparison is starker: packet.ai Dynamic at $3.75/hr against CoreWeave's $8.60/hr per-GPU on-demand rate, a 56% gap, even before CoreWeave's spot pricing which still requires accepting interruption.

- Dynamic: scheduler-enforced multi-tenant, single card, hourly. RTX 6000 Pro at $0.66/hr, B200 at $3.75/hr. No node minimum, no multi-year commitment.
- Dedicated: a whole card, single-tenant, 99% SLA. RTX 4090 at $0.39/hr, L40S at $0.92/hr, A100 80GB at $1.43/hr, B200 at $6.99/hr.

...

Billing is hourly with monthly commits up to 20% off. There are no platform fees and no ingress charges; egress is $0.04/GB. Up to 2 TB of local NVMe per node is included. Dynamic instances are SSH-ready in under five minutes, Dedicated in five to ten. Capacity is live in the US (California, Virginia, Texas, Oregon) and Europe (Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Paris, London, Dublin). H100 SXM, H200 and RTX 5090 are on the notify list.

...

Published starting rates in USD per GPU-hour, on-demand unless noted. Percentages compare the first price in each cell.

| Category | packet.ai YOU | CoreWeave |

| B200 (180–192GB) | $3.75/hr Dynamic · $6.99/hr Dedicated−56% | $8.60/hr on-demand per GPU (8× node) · $4.26/hr spot |
| RTX 6000 Pro (96GB) | $0.66/hr Dynamic−74% | $2.50/hr reserved only |

| Smallest unit | 1 GPU, hourly | Typically 8-GPU instance |

| Orchestration | SSH instances, API, packet CLI; bring your own K8s or Slurm | Managed Kubernetes (CKS), SUNK Slurm, Tensorizer |
| Data transfer | No ingress fee; egress $0.04/GB | Free egress |
| Time to capacity | Under 5 min (Dynamic); clusters 2–6 weeks | Minutes for on-demand nodes when available; contracts for scale |

### Pricing: two different units

CoreWeave publishes prices for 8-GPU HGX instances. Divide by eight and the B200 is $8.60/hr per GPU; packet.ai sells the same card at $3.75/hr Dynamic and $6.99/hr Dedicated. Even CoreWeave's spot B200 at $4.26/hr is above packet.ai's non-interruptible Dynamic rate. The A100 80GB is $2.70/hr on CoreWeave against $1.43/hr on packet.ai.

Those gaps narrow sharply under a CoreWeave contract. A 60% committed-use discount takes the B200 to roughly $3.44/hr, in the same range as packet.ai's own 12-month cluster pricing of $2.80–3.20/GPU-hr. In other words: at 64+ nodes on multi-year terms, the two converge. Below that, packet.ai is a fraction of the on-demand cost.

...

CoreWeave publishes list rates but most customers operate on negotiated contracts. The published on-demand H100 SXM rate is around $2.89/hr but reserved pricing for large clusters is lower and not public. packet.ai publishes every rate - Dynamic and Dedicated - with no hidden tiers.

...

Can I get a B200 from CoreWeave without a reservation?+

CoreWeave's B200 capacity is primarily reserved cluster inventory. On-demand B200 access exists but is limited and not guaranteed. packet.ai lists B200 Dynamic at $3.75/hr and B200 Dedicated at $6.99/hr as self-serve on-demand with no reservation required.

The pricing differential between neoclouds and hyperscalers is substantial. Lambda offers NVIDIA H100 instances at approximately $3.29 per hour, undercutting hyperscalers by roughly 23% for equivalent hardware. Broader market analysis puts the overall neocloud pricing advantage at 30% to 60% compared to hyperscaler equivalents, with neoclouds offering transparent pricing and long-term multi-year take-or-pay contracts rather than the complex variable pricing models hyperscalers use.

Nebius reports 20% to 25% lower total cost of ownership compared to hyperscalers, attributed to its infrastructure efficiency and custom designs. For enterprises running large-scale, sustained AI workloads where compute cost is a significant budget line, this pricing differential translates into material savings.

results.title: Computable GPU Index wants to be the CPI of AI compute — Tessera
highlights:
The Computable GPU Index launches as an open-source price tracker for GPU compute. What it gets right, what it misses, and why the AI economy needs it.

 Tessera Newsroom · 6 min read · September 2, 2026 

The gist

- The Computable GPU Index (CGI) is the first open-source, auditable price index for GPU compute, aggregating and normalizing listed prices across providers to a per-GPU-hour basis.
- It launches as GPU supply loosens, enabling price competition, but faces challenges in coverage, timeliness, and methodology for normalizing diverse instance types.
- The index won't capture negotiated wholesale deals, but aims to be a consistent, transparent reference point, shifting buyer leverage and becoming the default citation for GPU costs.

GPU compute has a pricing problem so severe that most buyers navigate it blind. Cloud vendors quote per-hour rates that vary by region, by instance family, by commitment term, and by whether you are buying reserved capacity or spot. Third-party resellers broker H100 clusters at prices that move weekly. Nobody publishes a consolidated, comparable number. The Computable GPU Index (CGI) launched this week as the first open-source price index for GPU compute, and it is trying to become the CPI of the AI hardware market.

The pitch is straightforward. CGI aggregates listed prices for GPU instances across major cloud providers and resellers, normalizes them to a per-GPU-hour basis, and publishes the result as an open dataset. Anyone can inspect the methodology, fork the code, or contribute new sources. The project launched on Product Hunt with a Discussion post attached, which suggests the team behind it wants community input on what gets indexed and how.

...

There are real questions about whether the CGI can deliver on its promise. The first is coverage. GPU pricing is fragmented across dozens of providers, each with its own instance naming conventions, region multipliers, and discount structures. An index that misses the long tail of resellers will produce a distorted picture. The second is timeliness. Spot prices fluctuate by the hour; committed-use discounts change quarterly. An index that updates weekly will be stale for the most volatile segments. The third is methodology. Normalizing a p4d.24xlarge on AWS against an A100-80GB node on a reseller platform requires assumptions about utilization, power costs, and amortization that reasonable people will dispute.

# Los precios del alquiler de GPU de NVIDIA suben a partir del 6 de Septiembre; el B200 aumenta un 11,65 % al mes y la RTX5090 se dispara un 28,57 %.

06/09/2026 01:40:03

Según Jin10, al 6 de Septiembre, los precios de alquiler de las GPU de NVIDIA mostraron un comportamiento mixto, aunque la mayoría de los Activos registró subidas. La tarifa de alquiler de la GPU B200 se situó en 6,42 dólares por hora, un 0,31 % más en el día y un 11,65 % más en el mes. La H100 subió a 3,06 dólares por hora, con un avance diario del 5,88 % y mensual del 12,50 %. La A100 se situó en 1,09 dólares por hora, un 2,83 % más en el día. La tarifa de alquiler de la RTX5090 alcanzó 0,63 dólares por hora, con el mejor desempeño: una subida semanal del 18,87 % y un repunte mensual del 28,57 %. La H200 cotizó a 4,55 dólares por hora, un 1,73 % menos en el día, pese a registrar un avance semanal del 2,48 %.

results.title: Sébastien Laye : quand la puissance de calcul s'empare des marchés financiers - Valeurs actuelles
highlights:
Il y a encore deux ans, affirmer que la puissance de calcul informatique deviendrait une matière première comparable au pétrole relevait volontiers de l’hyperbole technologique. En cette rentrée 2026, cette proposition est en train de devenir une réalité financière. Le 5 octobre prochain, sous réserve du feu vert réglementaire, le Chicago Mercantile Exchange, le plus important marché mondial de produits dérivés, doit lancer avec Silicon Data les premiers contrats à terme standardisés sur la location de puissance de calcul des GPU Nvidia H100 et B200. Quelques mois auparavant, Intercontinental Exchange, propriétaire du New York Stock Exchange, avait annoncé une initiative concurrente avec la start-up Ornn. Le 19 août, la Commodity Futures Trading Commission américaine est allée encore plus loin en ouvrant officiellement une consultation sur la réglementation des produits dérivés ayant pour sous-jacent le compute, c’est-à-dire la capacité de calcul utilisée par l’intelligence artificielle. La financiarisation de l‘intelligence artificielle vient de franchir une étape décisive.

...

Or cette énergie numérique est devenue à la fois rare, chère et extraordinairement difficile à évaluer. Deux entreprises peuvent aujourd’hui louer exactement le même type de GPU à des prix extrêmement différents en fonction de leur fournisseur, de la durée du contrat, de la localisation du centre de données, du niveau d’interconnexion entre les puces ou simplement du moment où elles ont négocié leur contrat. C’est précisément le genre d’opacité qui, dans l’histoire économique, précède généralement la création d’un marché organisé.
